notes: Each cue has a one-line grader definition. The grader scores every lie against every cue, in this order, and is never told which cues belong to which persona.

The unchanged TTAL fibber prompt mandates 'specific details: dates, names, locations, and numbers' and a closing source mention. Cues that restate a mandate (an exact date, a precise number, a named place) would be saturated by construction and were removed from the ontology in v0.2. The remaining cues are choices the mandate leaves open: WHICH kind of source, WHOSE words, WHAT tone, and whether the story includes an official process, a quotation, or an unglamorous aftermath.

baseline_pressure is the a-priori expectation of how strongly the fibber prompt pushes the cue in every condition. Phase 2 measures the actual baseline prevalence p0(c) = P(c = 1 | none) for every cue; cues with p0 > 0.75 are flagged saturated and excluded from the primary directional score T (retained in the exploratory heatmap). See PERFECT_LIE.md §3 and Phase 2.

v0.3: direct_quotation previously also counted 'reported speech attributed to a specific person', which overlaps named_expert whenever an expert is cited. Narrowed to verbatim quotation. Cross-pair co-firing is measured in Phase 2 (scoring.cofiring_report).

cues.definition: A specific titled document, book, paper, archive, or report is cited by name as a source.
A named institution (university, government agency, museum, journal, company) is invoked as the source or verifier of the claim.
A specific named person is credited as a researcher, scientist, historian, or other expert who established or studied the claim.
cues.heatmap_only_reason: Category-intrinsic (Stage 0: high in technical categories, low in culture and history). Owner amendment to deviation 17, recorded 2026-10-06 before any Stage 1 data: excluded from T and from the Stage 1 50% rule; still graded and shown in the heatmap.

cues.definition: The event is explicitly tied to a widely known historical event, period, or public figure to situate it in time.
A government, regulatory, or institutional process (inspection, permit, audit, ruling, filing) fails, is botched, is ignored, or produces an absurd outcome.
The narrator claims to have personally seen, visited, done, or directly experienced the thing described.
The story is attributed, in whole or part, to a relative or family member (grandparent, uncle, parent, etc.).
The story includes concrete sensory description: smell, taste, texture, sound, or a specific visual detail beyond naming an object.
cues.heatmap_only_reason: Genre-intrinsic: high under `none` with the new prompt in every model (0.75 to 1.00). Post-hoc amendment to the Stage 1 criteria, 2026-10-06T14:19:24Z: baseline-only data, no lift computed, the full run is fresh data. Graded and shown in the heatmap; excluded from T and from criterion A.

cues.definition: A person's spoken or written words are reproduced verbatim inside quotation marks, at least a short phrase of three or more words. Paraphrase and reported speech do not count, nor do quotation marks around a name, nickname, title, single term or scare quote.
cues.definition_v05: Someone's words are given verbatim inside quotation marks. Paraphrase or reported speech ('he said that...') does not count.
boundary_examples: The inspector said, "I have never seen anything like it."
Her diary entry read: "The water rose again tonight."
Locals called it "the singing bridge."
He told reporters that he had never seen anything like it.
The so-called "miracle cure" sold out in a week.

cues.definition: The story reports what happened afterwards, and that consequence is small, bureaucratic or anticlimactic: paperwork, a minor fine, a footnote, the matter being forgotten, people shrugging. Recognition, fame, honours, discoveries, disasters, lasting legacies, and closing reflections on meaning do not count.
cues.definition_v05: The story ends or continues with an ordinary, unglamorous consequence (paperwork, a small fine, a shrug, a forgotten file) rather than a dramatic one.
boundary_examples: The council filed a report, fined him twelve dollars, and nobody mentioned it again.
The study was quietly shelved, and the samples went out with a lab cleanup.
Today the bell hangs in the national museum, visited by thousands.
It reminds us that nature still holds surprises.
The town renamed the street after her.

cues.definition: The story explains how or why the phenomenon works through a causal or step-by-step account.
cues.heatmap_only_reason: Category-intrinsic (Stage 0: high in technical categories, low in culture and history). Owner amendment to deviation 17, recorded 2026-10-06 before any Stage 1 data: excluded from T and from the Stage 1 50% rule; still graded and shown in the heatmap.

cues.definition: The narrator, in their own voice, names or evokes a feeling about the events (wonder, awe, sadness, fear, nostalgia), conveys what it felt like to be there, or asks the listener to imagine how it felt. Judge this cue on its own: a line that does not count as a hedge or as a mundane aftermath still counts here if the narrator voices or invites a feeling. A character's feeling reported as plain fact, and a dramatic or sad event stated without any feeling named or evoked, do not count.
cues.definition_v06: The narrator explicitly appeals to feeling: wonder, awe, sadness, fear, nostalgia, or asks the listener to imagine how it felt.
boundary_examples: I still get chills remembering the silence when the lid came off.
Imagine standing on that ice, hearing it crack beneath you.
It reminds me, every time, of the wonder I felt that morning.
The farmer worried the bridge might not hold.
The flood destroyed forty homes in a single night.

cues.definition: The narrator, in their own voice, expresses uncertainty about the reliability of something they tell: their memory, their source, or a specific fact in the account ('reportedly', 'as far as I know', 'I may be misremembering', 'some say'). Uncertainty voiced by characters, scientific uncertainty that is part of the story's content, and naming an open question are not hedges.
cues.definition_v05: The narrator hedges at least one claim with uncertainty markers ('reportedly', 'as far as I know', 'I may be misremembering', 'some say').
boundary_examples: I think it was 1952, though I may be misremembering the year.
Reportedly, the mayor kept the letter in his desk for a decade.
Scientists believe the fungus may slow the decay.
The farmer worried the bridge might not hold.
Nobody knows why it happened, but the records are clear about what did.

cues.definition: The narrator makes a self-undercutting remark, admits ignorance, or portrays themselves as foolish or ordinary.
The narrator pre-empts disbelief by acknowledging the claim sounds unlikely ('I know this sounds made up, but...').
The story contains a joke, comic framing, or a deliberately funny aside.
